title: Defining Survival Distributions
text: define_surv_param function allows define parametric survival model specified distribution parameter values. Parameterization based flexsurv package.
code: param_surv <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   print(param_surv) #> A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3).

title: Defining Survival Distributions
text: define_surv_cure function allows define parametric mixture/non-mixture cure model specified distribution, cure fraction, parameter values.
code: cure_surv <- define_surv_cure('exp', theta = 0.21, rate = 0.04, mixture = TRUE)   print(cure_surv) #> An exponential mixture cure distribution (theta = 0.21, rate = 0.04).

title: Defining Survival Distributions
text: define_surv_spline function allows define Royston & Parmar restricted cubic spline model specified scale, parameter values, knot times.
code: spline_dist <- define_surv_spline(     scale = 'hazard', # spline used to model log cumulative hazards     -2.08, 2.75, 0.23, # parameters     -1.62, 0.57, 1.191 # knot times   )   print(spline_dist) #> A Royston & Parmar spline model of log cumulative hazard with 3 knots (gamma = [-2.08, 2.75, 0.23], knots = [-1.62, 0.57, 1.19]).

title: Defining Survival Distributions
text: define_surv_km function allows define survival distribution based times survival probabilities Kaplan-Meier.
code: km_output <- data.frame(     times = c(0, 2, 5, 10, 17, 21),     surv_prob = c(1, 0.98, 0.94, 0.89, 0.78, 0.78)   )   km_dist <- define_surv_km(km_output, "times", "surv_prob")   print(km_dist) #> A Kaplan-Meier distribution: #>    time survival #>   <dbl>    <dbl> #> 1     0     1    #> 2     2     0.98 #> 3     5     0.94 #> 4    10     0.89 #> 5    17     0.78 #> 6    21     0.78

title: Defining Survival Distributions
text: define_surv_lifetable function allows define survival distribution based life-table, starting age, gender mix.
code: life_table <- data.frame(     age_in_years = c(50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55),     p_death_male = c(0.0021, 0.0022, 0.0022, 0.0023, 0.0022, 0.0024),     p_death_female = c(0.0018, 0.0018, 0.0018, 0.0019, 0.0019, 0.0020)   )   lifetable_dist <- define_surv_lifetable(     life_table, # data.frame containing life-table     51, # starting age     0.48, # percent male     age_col = 'age_in_years', # column in life-table containing age     male_col = 'p_death_male', # column in life-table containing male p(death)     female_col = 'p_death_female' # column in life-table containing female p(death)   )   print(lifetable_dist) #> A life-table survival distribution (48.0% male, 52.0% female): #>     age   male female #>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> #> 1    51 0.0022 0.0018 #> 2    52 0.0022 0.0018 #> 3    53 0.0023 0.0019 #> 4    54 0.0022 0.0019 #> 5    55 0.0024 0.002

title: Defining Survival Distributions
text: define_surv_func function allows define survival distribution based custom function.
code: custom_dist <- define_surv_func(function(t) pweibull(t, 1.2, 20.1, lower.tail = FALSE))   print(custom_dist) #> A survival distribution based on a custom function #>   Function: #>     function (t)  #>     pweibull(t, 1.2, 20.1, lower.tail = FALSE)

title: Defining Survival Distributions
text: addition functions provided openqalysurv, can use survival distributions created supported third-party packages.
code: library(survival)   library(flexsurv)   survfit_dist <- survfit(Surv(recyrs, censrec)~1, data = bc)   flexsurv_dist <- flexsurvreg(Surv(recyrs, censrec)~1, data = bc, dist = 'lnorm')

title: Generating Predictions
text: Predicted survival probabilities can generated given survival distribution set times using surv_prob function.

title: Generating Predictions
text: Event probabilities can generated given survival distributon set time intervals using event_prob function.

title: Modifying & Combining Distributions
text: Hazard ratios can applied survival distribution using apply_hr function.
code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   dist2 <- apply_hr(dist1, 0.85)   print(dist2) #> A proportional hazards survival distribution: #>     * Hazard Ratio: 0.85 #>     * Baseline Distribution: A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3).

title: Modifying & Combining Distributions
text: Odds ratios can applied survival distribution using apply_or function.
code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   dist2 <- apply_or(dist1, 0.45)   print(dist2) #> A proportional odds survival distribution: #>     * Odds Ratio: 0.45 #>     * Baseline Distribution: A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3).

title: Modifying & Combining Distributions
text: Accleration factors, proportionally scale event times, can applied using apply_af function.
code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   dist2 <- apply_af(dist1, 0.75)   print(dist2) #> An accelerated failure time survival distribution: #>     * Acceleration Factor: 0.75 #>     * Baseline Distribution: A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3).

title: Modifying & Combining Distributions
text: Hazards distribution can shifted forward backward fixed amount time using apply_shift function. Note positive value shift move hazards forward negative value shift hazards backward (resulting initial period event risk).
code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   dist2 <- apply_shift(dist1, 2.1)   print(dist2) #> A shifted survival distribution: #>     * Shift: 2.1 #>     * Baseline Distribution: A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3).

title: Modifying & Combining Distributions
text: Survival distributions can mixed according specified weights using mix function.
code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   dist2 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.4, scale = 4.1)   dist3 <- mix(dist1, 0.8, dist2, 0.2) # Mix of 80% dist1 and 20% dist2   print(dist3) #> A mixed survival distribution: #>     * Distribution 1 (80%): A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3). #>     * Distribution 2 (20%): A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.4, scale = 4.1).

title: Modifying & Combining Distributions
text: Survival distributions can joined together specified cutpoints using join function.
code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   dist2 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.4, scale = 4.1)   dist3 <- join(dist1, 3, dist2) # Join dist2 and dist3 at time 3   print(dist3) #> A joined survival distribution: #>     * Segment 1 (t = 0 - 3): A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3). #>     * Segment 2 (t = 3 - ∞): A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.4, scale = 4.1).

title: Modifying & Combining Distributions
text: Survival distributions can combined independent risks using add_hazards function. results survival distribution survival function equal product survival functions combined distributions.
code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   dist2 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.4, scale = 4.1)   dist3 <- add_hazards(dist1, dist2) # combined hazards of dist1 and dist2   print(dist3) #> A survival distribution combining the hazards of: #>     * Distribution 1: A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3). #>     * Distribution 2: A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.4, scale = 4.1).

title: Modifying & Combining Distributions
text: Models fitted using survfit flexsurvreg predictors can used generate survival distribution representing subject set subjects using set_covariates.
code: library(flexsurv) #> Loading required package: survival library(tibble)  # Fit a model using bc dataset using good as predictor print(as_tibble(bc)) #> # A tibble: 686 × 4 #>    censrec rectime group recyrs #>      <int>   <int> <fct>  <dbl> #>  1       0    1342 Good    3.68 #>  2       0    1578 Good    4.32 #>  3       0    1760 Good    4.82 #>  4       0    1152 Good    3.16 #>  5       0     967 Good    2.65 #>  6       0     629 Good    1.72 #>  7       0     461 Good    1.26 #>  8       1     991 Good    2.72 #>  9       0     758 Good    2.08 #> 10       0    1617 Good    4.43 #> # title: Getting Started
text: openqalysurv package contains number functions defining survival distributions various types. example, define_surv_param function allows define parametric survival distribution given family given parameter values. information kinds survival distributions supported openqalysurv can found “Defining Survival Distributions” vignette.

code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('exp', rate = 0.013)   print(dist1) #> An exponential distribution (rate = 0.013).

title: Getting Started

title: Getting Started
text: Survival probabilities distribution can graphed using plot method.
code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   plot(dist1, max_time = 20)

title: Getting Started
text: Survival distributions can modified using variety functions provided openqalysurv. example, apply_hr function can used apply hazard ratio survival distribution. also possible combine multiple survival distributions one. example, join function allows two survival distributions joined specified cutpoint.
code: dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   dist2 <- apply_hr(dist1, 0.45)   print(dist2) #> A proportional hazards survival distribution: #>     * Hazard Ratio: 0.45 #>     * Baseline Distribution: A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3). dist1 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3)   dist2 <- define_surv_param('weibull', shape = 1.4, scale = 4.1)   dist3 <- join(dist1, 3, dist2) # Join dist2 and dist3 at time 3   print(dist3) #> A joined survival distribution: #>     * Segment 1 (t = 0 - 3): A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.2, scale = 5.3). #>     * Segment 2 (t = 3 - ∞): A Weibull (AFT) distribution (shape = 1.4, scale = 4.1).

title: Getting Started
text: complicated survival distributions can created stringing together multiple openqalysurv operations. Use %>% operator magrittr supported.
code: # create an exponential distribution   dist1 <- define_surv_param('exp', rate = 0.04)      # create a survival distribution based on custom function   dist2 <- define_surv_func(function(t) pweibull(t, 1.2, 20.1, lower.tail = FALSE))    # create a Royston & Parmar spline model   dist3 <- define_surv_spline(     scale = 'hazard', # spline used to model log cumulative hazards     -2.08, 2.75, 0.23, # parameters     -1.62, 0.57, 1.191   )    dist4 <- dist1 %>% # take dist1       apply_hr(0.4) %>% # apply a hazard ratio of 0.4 to it       join(4, dist2) %>% # join it to dist2 at time 4       mix(0.25, dist3, 0.75) # mix the result with dist4 with weights of 25% and 75% respectively    print(dist4) #> A mixed survival distribution: #>     * Distribution 1 (25%):  #>         A joined survival distribution: #>             * Segment 1 (t = 0 - 4):  #>                 A proportional hazards survival distribution: #>                     * Hazard Ratio: 0.4 #>                     * Baseline Distribution: An exponential distribution (rate = 0.04). #>             * Segment 2 (t = 4 - ∞):  #>                 A survival distribution based on a custom function #>                   Function: #>                     function (t)  #>                     pweibull(t, 1.2, 20.1, lower.tail = FALSE) #>     * Distribution 2 (75%): A Royston & Parmar spline model of log cumulative hazard with 3 knots (gamma = [-2.08, 2.75, 0.23], knots = [-1.62, 0.57, 1.19]).

title: Apply Fixed Shift in Time — apply_shift
text: shifted survival function defined : $$S_{\mathrm{shifted}}(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & t \le \delta \\ S(t - \delta) & t > \delta \end{cases}$$ \(\delta\) shift amount \(S\) baseline survival function. positive shift delays hazards \(\delta\) time units (curve moves right); negative shift accelerates (curve moves left). common use apply_shift realign timescale distribution passing join. distribution estimated data begins cut point \(c\) — time zero corresponds \(c\) — applying apply_shift(dist, c) maps internal time absolute study timescale, join requires.

title: Apply Time-Dependent Hazard Ratio — apply_td_hr
text: dist survival distribution time numeric vector time points corresponding hazard ratio hr numeric vector hazard ratios (must length time, length 1) log_hr optional argument (defaults FALSE) indicate provided hazard ratios log scale

title: Apply Time-Dependent Hazard Ratio — apply_td_hr
text: surv_td_ph object length(hr) > 1, otherwise delegates apply_hr.

title: Apply Time-Dependent Hazard Ratio — apply_td_hr
text: time hr vectors parallel: hr[] hazard ratio applies time[]. Duplicate (time, hr) pairs allowed deduplicated. However, conflicting HRs time point (.e., time different HR values) cause error. Interaction apply_af: (1) Composition order affects HR applies given query time: apply_af(apply_td_hr(dist, time, hr), af): HR intervals accelerated time apply_td_hr(apply_af(dist, af), time, hr): HR intervals query time (2) Acceleration factors affect HR granularity. wrapping AFT distribution af < 1, unit HR interval spans larger portion baseline survival curve, reducing effective precision time-dependent effects.

Define Parametric Mixture or Non-Mixture Cure Distribution — define_surv_cure

See details listing valid distributions. theta numeric value [0, 1] representing cure fraction, .e. long-term probability never experiencing event. ... Additional distribution parameters (see details section ) mixture logical determining whether mixture non-mixture model defined.

title: Define Parametric Mixture or Non-Mixture Cure Distribution — define_surv_cure
text: Mixture cure model (mixture = TRUE): $$S(t) = \theta + (1 - \theta) \, S_u(t)$$ Non-mixture cure model (mixture = FALSE): $$S(t) = \theta^{F_u(t)}$$ \(\theta\) cure fraction (long-term survival probability), \(S_u(t)\) survival function uncured subgroup, \(F_u(t) = 1 - S_u(t)\) corresponding CDF. Supported distributions uncured subgroup listed table .

title: Define Parametric Distribution (flexsurv Parameterization) — define_surv_flexsurv
text: Exponential: S(t) = exp(-rate * t) Weibull (AFT): S(t) = exp(-(t / scale)^shape) Weibull (PH): S(t) = exp(-scale * t^shape) Lognormal: S(t) = 1 - Phi((log(t) - meanlog) / sdlog) Phi() standard normal CDF Log-logistic: S(t) = 1 / (1 + (t / scale)^shape) Gompertz: hazard h(t) = rate * exp(shape * t), survival S(t) = exp(-(rate / shape) * (exp(shape * t) - 1)) Gamma: closed-form survival function; computed numerically via pgamma() Generalized gamma (stable/original): simple closed form; see Prentice (1974) Stacy (1962) Generalized F (stable/original): simple closed form; see Prentice (1975)

what: Define Fractional Polynomial Survival Distribution — define_surv_fp
title: Define Fractional Polynomial Survival Distribution — define_surv_fp
text: Define fractional polynomial (FP) survival distribution log-hazard scale, used network meta-analysis survival data. Supports FP1 (one power) FP2 (two powers) models.

title: Define Fractional Polynomial Survival Distribution — define_surv_fp
Define Fractional Polynomial Survival Distribution — define_surv_fp
text: betas numeric vector coefficients. Length must equal length(powers) + 1 (intercept plus one per power). powers numeric vector fractional polynomial powers (length 1 FP1, length 2 FP2).

title: Define Fractional Polynomial Survival Distribution — define_surv_fp
text: surv_fp object.

title: Define Fractional Polynomial Survival Distribution — define_surv_fp
text: log-hazard modeled : FP1: log h(t) = beta0 + beta1 * t^(p1) FP2: log h(t) = beta0 + beta1 * t^(p1) + beta2 * t^(p2) t^0 = log(t) convention, repeated powers use Royston-Altman convention multiplying log(t). Survival probabilities computed S(t) = exp(-H(t)) H(t) cumulative hazard obtained numerical integration hazard function. standard power set {-2, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3}, real-valued powers accepted.

title: Define Fractional Polynomial Survival Distribution — define_surv_fp
text: Jansen, J. P. (2011). Network meta-analysis survival data fractional polynomials. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 11, 61. Royston, P. Altman, D.G. (1994). Regression using fractional polynomials continuous covariates: parsimonious parametric modelling. Journal Royal Statistical Society Series C, 43, 429-467.

title: Define Fractional Polynomial Survival Distribution — define_surv_fp
code: # FP1 model define_surv_fp(betas = c(-3, 0.5), powers = c(1)) #> An FP1 survival distribution (beta0 = -3.0, beta1 = 0.5, powers = [1]).  # FP2 model define_surv_fp(betas = c(-3, 0.5, -0.2), powers = c(0, 1)) #> An FP2 survival distribution (beta0 = -3.0, beta1 = 0.5, beta2 = -0.2, powers = [0, 1]).

title: Join Distributions — join
text: join ensures overall survival curve continuous cut point rescaling next distribution's survival values. single cut point \(c\) joining distributions \(S_1\) \(S_2\), joined survival function : $$S(t) = \begin{cases} S_1(t) & t \le c \\ \frac{S_1(c)}{S_2(c)} \cdot S_2(t) & t > c \end{cases}$$ Importantly, second distribution evaluated absolute time \(t\), \(t - c\). means join rescales survival probabilities continuity — shift remap timescale distribution. distributions passed join must therefore share time origin (typically time zero = study baseline). distribution estimated data begins cut point — time zero corresponds cut point — must first shifted apply_shift realign timescales: Without shift, join evaluate distribution absolute time \(t\) instead intended \(t - c\), producing incorrect survival estimates beyond cut point.
code: # dist_from_cutpoint was fit to data starting at t = c # (its time zero = the cut point) shifted <- apply_shift(dist_from_cutpoint, c) joined  <- join(km, c, shifted)
